bridges.mechanism: A sustained rise in attacks on commercial and naval shipping forces governments to reallocate immediate defense procurement and budgetary resources to naval patrols, convoy protection and port security, shrinking funds available for external assistance to Ukraine.

Frequent maritime attacks and visible disruptions to trade and energy flows increase domestic political pressure to prioritize national maritime and energy security, reducing public and parliamentary tolerance for sustained high-cost support to Ukraine.

Rising per-voyage costs (insurance, fuel, rerouting) raise input and working-capital costs for trade-exposed firms, worsening credit metrics and leading investors to demand wider corporate credit spreads.

Higher insurance premiums, rerouting and security surcharges materially raise transaction and logistics costs for exporters and project sponsors, causing private investors and funds to scale back or delay cross‑border capital commitments into technology and energy projects (including those channels that can be repurposed for DPRK procurement).

Sustained higher insurance, diversion and transit costs for specialized equipment and chemical inputs raises lead times and supply shortages for fabs, forcing lower wafer starts and temporary curtailment of advanced production capacity.

A sustained upward shock to benchmark oil prices feeds directly into headline inflation and inflation expectations, prompting central banks to tighten monetary policy and raise short-term policy rates to anchor inflation.

A rapid rise in oil benchmark prices increases inflation and borrowing costs and diverts investor allocation toward energy and defensive assets, reducing near‑term VC and corporate capex available for AI infrastructure projects.

Expanded sanctions reduce correspondent-banking links and constrain market-makers' ability to intermediate cross-border bond trades, causing dealers to pull back and reducing observable bond-market liquidity.

Tighter sanctions increase counterparty, settlement and trade-risk for internationally active firms (and their banks), reducing access to funding and increasing perceived default risk, which pushes corporate spreads wider.

Stronger and more rigorously enforced sanctions against Iran/Houthi-related entities prompt correspondent banks and institutional investors to de‑risk by withdrawing or restricting foreign capital exposures, reducing net cross‑border flows into sectors and intermediaries that could be exploited by DPRK networks.

Escalation of sanctions tied to Iran/Houthi activity prompts the US and allies to broaden and more tightly enforce export‑control licensing and entity lists to prevent sanction circumvention and dual‑use flows — including preemptive restrictions that affect China‑linked supply chains.

A sustained rise in overall combat intensity increases operational interruptions, counterparty risk and default probability for firms (especially in Europe and energy‑sensitive sectors), so investors demand higher credit spreads on corporate bonds.

A marked increase in overall Russia–Ukraine kinetic intensity raises global maritime and geopolitical risk premia and prompts insurers and war‑risk underwriters to lift premiums and require more costly security measures, directly increasing per‑voyage operating costs for carriers in adjacent and global routes.

Escalating conflict disrupts production and logistics of critical inputs (e.g., semiconductor‑grade neon, specialty gases, transport routes) originating in or routed through the conflict region, causing downtime and reduced effective output at advanced fabs globally.

Rising conflict intensity raises commercial and compliance risk (insurance, sanctions exposure, due diligence burdens), prompting firms, universities and intermediaries to curtail or delay cross‑border transfers of technology, tooling and tacit expertise to higher‑risk foreign partners including Chinese entities.

Sharp increases in missile and drone strikes create episodic volatility and operational/settlement risks that prompt market‑makers to pull back and widen quotes, reducing bond market depth and liquidity.

A sustained spike in aerial strikes raises market perceptions of near‑term supply disruption risk (via possible export chokepoint damage and escalation spillovers), prompting traders to bid up benchmark crude prices on risk‑premium adjustments.

Increased available Russian defense funds are used to purchase missiles, components, and technical assistance from North Korean suppliers and to finance capacity upgrades, directly expanding DPRK factory throughput and production lines for offensive missiles.

Higher defense funding availability produces direct government procurement, grants and defense-contractor capex that is routed into AI compute, secure data centers and related infrastructure, increasing overall investment flows into AI infrastructure.

Stronger, visible political support from backer governments reduces perceived tail‑risk of spillovers and implicit credit risk for proximate developed economies, lowering risk premia and benchmark sovereign yields.

Rising political will among Western backers to sustain Ukraine leads to diversion of limited naval assets and rules‑of‑engagement political capital toward European deterrence, reducing patrols/deterrence in the Red Sea/Arabian Sea and thereby enabling more Houthi attacks and seizures.

Sustained high political support among Ukraine backers further isolates Russia, prompting Moscow to deepen reciprocal military-diplomatic cooperation with Pyongyang (e.g., security consultations, coordinated messaging, barter deals), thereby raising perceived strategic alignment.

Stronger domestic and allied political will to punish or isolate Russia leads governments to broaden and tighten export control regimes (and to coordinate allied controls), often extending scrutiny to dual‑use AI and semiconductor technologies relevant to US–China competition.

A rapid increase in global AI compute accelerates development and fielding of commercial and coalition AI maritime ISR, automatic sensor-fusion and real‑time targeting/cueing systems that improve detection and interdiction of small-boat and drone attacks, reducing successful Houthi/IRGC-linked incidents.

An increase in advanced fab capacity in a country reduces anticipated government support needs and improves growth/fiscal prospects for that jurisdiction, lowering its sovereign risk premium and benchmark yields over the medium term.

Large, rapid redirection of investor capital into AI infrastructure (equity placements, private infrastructure deals, and capex financing) mechanically withdraws tradable liquidity from bond desks and increases price impact for bond trades, reducing bond market liquidity.

An increase in cross‑border technology transfers lowers operational and adaptation risk for multinational tech firms (improving production flexibility and revenue prospects), which reduces perceived credit risk and compresses their corporate bond spreads.

Increased cross-border transfers of tacit knowledge, tooling designs and manufacturing practices (via diaspora engineers, contractors, or covert procurement networks) enable North Korean facilities to adopt higher-yield production techniques and scale production lines, raising missile output per unit time.

Increased cross‑border transfer of dual‑use AI software, navigation chips and tacit engineering know‑how to Russian procurement networks directly improves guidance, autonomy and endurance of loitering munitions and cruise/UCAV systems, raising the sustained rate of aerial strikes.

A sudden increase in export‑control intensity raises near‑term revenue and supply‑chain uncertainty for affected tech manufacturers and suppliers, prompting credit investors to reprice default and liquidity risk and demand wider corporate spreads.

A step-up in export controls tied to the US–China tech rivalry prompts allied regulatory coordination and intelligence sharing that expands targeted designations and trade/financial restrictions on intermediary firms and networks supplying Iran/Houthi proxies, raising sanctions and enforcement intensity.

Stricter US/China export controls directly block legal shipments and licensing of AI-relevant hardware, software and documentation to intermediaries and suppliers that would otherwise transfer dual-use capabilities to North Korean actors, reducing the speed and volume of technology diffusion.

Tightened export controls increase compliance, screening and legal risks for banks and investors, prompting intermediaries and private financiers to reduce transactions with flagged entities or jurisdictions and thereby lowering cross-border capital flows that could finance proliferation-related activities linked to North Korea.

A marked tightening of export controls on AI and semiconductor tech signals an escalatory US‑China contest and provokes allied policy narratives about strategic competition, which increases domestic political support among backers for sustained or expanded assistance to Ukraine.

A rapid rise in North Korea's missile production capacity increases the assessed probability of strikes and supply‑chain disruption for regional firms and insurers, causing investors to demand higher credit spreads on corporates with exposure to those risks.

An increase in North Korea's missile production capacity enables larger, faster shipments of complete missiles and missile components to Russia, directly enlarging Russia's munitions stockpiles and permitting a higher sustained rate of missile/loitering-munition strikes in Ukraine.

Credible intelligence or visible evidence of a sustained increase in North Korean missile industrial output triggers US administrative actions and diplomatic pressure on allied suppliers to broaden export restrictions on components and tooling used in missile guidance and propulsion, which spill over into tighter controls on related high‑end tech sent to China.

Greater ease and standardization in producing offensive weapons in North Korea leads to large, low‑cost exports of drones, rockets, or munitions to Russian forces and proxies, increasing the scale and geographic spread of kinetic operations across the theater.

Demonstrated mass‑producibility of weapons reliant on advanced compute or guidance chips leads the US and partner governments to tighten controls and pressure equipment and IP suppliers, slowing or cancelling fab expansions and technology transfers that would otherwise increase advanced semiconductor fabrication capacity accessible to China.

A sudden reduction in cross‑border capital flows into Asian and defence‑sensitive bond markets (driven by North Korean nuclear escalations) removes nonresident liquidity providers and raises margin/financing costs for dealers, materially reducing bond market depth and tradability.

Rising cross‑border capital flows routed through North Korean/Russian networks facilitate sanctions‑evasion and liquidity transfers that augment Russian access to funds or credit for military procurement, increasing readily available resources for defense operations.

Accelerated diffusion of dual‑use and maritime strike technologies from North Korea to Iranian networks or Houthi proxies directly enables more effective anti-ship missiles, unmanned surface/underwater vehicles and naval mines, increasing the frequency and lethality of attacks on vessels and port infrastructure.

A measurable increase in coordinated security alignment and posture among major powers in response to North Korean nuclear developments typically entails near‑term higher defence outlays and expected sovereign issuance, putting upward pressure on benchmark sovereign yields.

A demonstrable tightening of strategic alignment or formal cooperation between North Korea and Iran triggers rapid policy responses from the US/EU/allies (e.g., targeted secondary sanctions, shipping restrictions, and designation of facilitation networks), increasing the measured intensity of trade and financial restrictions on Iranian and associated actors.

A sharp escalation in North Korean nuclear activity drives closer US–Japan–ROK security coordination and coalitions that rapidly harmonize and expand export controls and licensing regimes targeting dual‑use and advanced tech flows to China.

Sustained increases in sovereign yields raise visible debt‑service burdens and consumer borrowing costs, driving domestic economic pain and electoral or public pressure that erodes political support for continued external involvement.

Rising sovereign yields increase governments' debt‑service burdens and the cost of sovereign‑backed loans or guarantees, making states more likely to delay or shrink subsidy and guarantee packages that underwrite new advanced fab projects, slowing fabrication capacity expansion.

Widening corporate spreads signal higher counterparty and funding risk, prompting correspondent banks and shipping/service providers to tighten compliance and de-risk by refusing or restricting Iran-related transactions, which effectively raises the intensity of trade and financial restrictions.

Widening corporate credit spreads raise borrowing and trade‑finance costs for component manufacturers and assemblers in regional supplier countries, constraining their output and exports of precision parts and thereby reducing North Korea's aggregate missile production capacity.

Widening corporate credit spreads increase financing costs and liquidity strain for cloud providers and hardware vendors, prompting them to defer big GPU/TPU orders and slow cluster expansions, reducing near‑term growth in global AI compute capacity.

Raised policy rates in major economies reduce near-term demand expectations for oil and increase the discount rate applied to future cash flows, exerting downward pressure on benchmark crude prices within months.

Higher policy rates raise sovereign borrowing costs and near‑term fiscal financing pressures, making governments more reluctant or slower to approve new defense appropriations and external aid tranches for the war.

Higher short‑term policy rates raise borrowing costs and discount rates, directly reducing venture funding, corporate capex approvals and debt financing for AI datacenters and hardware purchases, cutting capital flows into AI infrastructure.

A sudden drop in bond-market liquidity forces banks and insurers to hoard capital and withdraw trade-finance/insurance capacity, prompting immediate rises in letters-of-credit fees and war-risk/PDV insurance premiums that raise per-voyage shipping costs.

Improved bond market liquidity lowers the cost and risk of short-term financing (eg repo, working capital) for trading houses and brokers that procure and move dual‑use components, increasing the speed at which such technologies diffuse into gray‑market channels that can reach North Korea.

Deteriorating bond and credit market liquidity raises transaction costs and elevates financing and counterparty risk for cross‑border M&A, joint ventures and supplier contracts, causing firms to curtail overseas R&D partnerships and personnel exchanges that transmit tacit technology.

When investors rapidly rebalance away from emerging/illiquid assets into safe cash or home-market securities, net international private and institutional capital available for technology and energy sectors falls, directly reducing cross‑border capital flow rates that could finance intermediaries or suppliers linked to DPRK procurement.

Crude oil supply flow
nodes.description: Net physical rate at which crude oil is produced and made available to global markets (barrels per day).

nodes.label: Refined fuels flow
nodes.description: Net rate at which refined petroleum products (diesel, gasoline, fuel oil) are delivered into distribution and export channels.

nodes.label: Strategic petroleum reserve level
nodes.description: Aggregate stock level of publicly held strategic oil reserves available for release to stabilize markets (volume).

nodes.label: Refinery throughput rate
nodes.description: Rate at which refining capacity converts crude into refined products (percentage of capacity utilized or barrels per day).

nodes.label: Maritime security incident frequency
nodes.description: Rate of hostile actions, strikes, seizures, or major accidents affecting vessels and infrastructure in key sea lanes (incidents per time).

nodes.label: Geopolitical escalation pressure
nodes.description: Intensity of ongoing geopolitical/military confrontation that raises the probability of further disruptive actions (qualitative-to-quantitative index).

nodes.label: Maritime transit capacity
nodes.description: Effective throughput capacity of key maritime routes and chokepoints measured as maximum safe transit volume per time.

nodes.label: Waterway draft availability
nodes.description: Average navigable water depth/draft availability limiting vessel size and cargo per transit in critical canals and straits (meters or relative index).

nodes.label: Average shipping reroute distance/time
nodes.description: Additional distance or transit time required on average when vessels avoid high-risk routes (nautical miles or hours).

nodes.label: Shipping operating costs and insurance
nodes.description: Average per-voyage incremental costs including fuel, insurance premiums, security and diversion costs faced by maritime carriers.

nodes.label: Global oil and product trade volume
nodes.description: Aggregate volume of crude and refined product flows crossing borders and sea lanes per time period.

nodes.label: Benchmark oil market price level
nodes.description: prevailing benchmark price level for crude oil used in price formation and contracts (e.g., $/barrel index).

nodes.label: Price discovery volatility and risk premium
nodes.description: Measured volatility and market-implied risk premium that affect short-term price swings and hedging costs.

nodes.label: Sanctions and trade-restriction intensity
nodes.description: Degree to which trade, shipping and financial restrictions are applied and enforced, affecting legal access to markets and services.

nodes.label: Financial channel disruption
nodes.description: Extent to which payment, banking and settlement channels for energy trade are impaired or rerouted (access and speed).

nodes.label: Demand elasticity for fuels
nodes.description: Price responsiveness of consumption for oil and refined fuels across major end uses (percentage change in demand per percent price change).

Conflict intensity
nodes.description: Measures the aggregate level of ongoing military violence and kinetic operations across the theatre (including scale and geographic spread of engagements).

nodes.label: Aerial strike rate
nodes.description: Measures the continuous rate of missile and unmanned aerial system strikes launched into or across the conflict area.

nodes.label: Ground offensive activity
nodes.description: Measures the frequency and scale of ground maneuver operations and offensive actions by armed formations.

nodes.label: Arms transfer flow
nodes.description: Measures the volumetric rate and tempo at which military equipment and weapons are delivered into the conflict system.

nodes.label: Defense production capacity
nodes.description: Measures the available industrial output capacity to manufacture, repair, or supply military systems and munitions.

nodes.label: Defense funding availability
nodes.description: Measures the stock of financial resources committed or readily available to support military operations and external assistance.

nodes.label: Mediator diplomatic engagement
nodes.description: Measures the intensity and frequency of third‑party mediation actions, contacts, and formal negotiation initiatives.

nodes.label: Negotiation trust
nodes.description: Measures the perceived mutual confidence and credibility between negotiating sides that commitments will be honored.

nodes.label: Political will among backers
nodes.description: Measures the level of domestic political support in external supporter populations and governments for sustaining involvement.

nodes.label: Economic strain on supporters
nodes.description: Measures the degree of fiscal and macroeconomic stress in jurisdictions providing financial or material support that constrains continued assistance.

nodes.label: Sanctions pressure
nodes.description: Measures the intensity and effective economic impact of targeted restrictive measures on actor economies and decision calculus.

nodes.label: Information warfare intensity
nodes.description: Measures the volume and aggressiveness of psychological operations, propaganda, diplomatic signaling, and information disruptions.

nodes.label: Supply chain stability
nodes.description: Measures the continuity and reliability of logistical routes and material flows that sustain military and humanitarian operations.

nodes.label: Troop morale
nodes.description: Measures the prevailing morale, cohesion, and willingness to fight among military personnel engaged in the conflict.

nodes.label: Civilian harm and displacement rate
nodes.description: Measures the rate at which civilian casualties, injuries, and forced displacements are occurring over time.

nodes.label: Negotiation readiness
nodes.description: Measures the operational and institutional readiness of parties and mediators to enter, sustain, and implement formal talks and agreements.

Global AI compute capacity
nodes.description: The aggregate available compute resources (GPU/TPU cycles, cluster throughput) that can be allocated to AI training and inference worldwide.

nodes.label: Advanced semiconductor fabrication capacity
nodes.description: The installed production capability for advanced process-node semiconductors (wafer starts, output of critical chips) available to AI hardware supply chains.

nodes.label: Capital flows into AI infrastructure
nodes.description: The rate and volume of investment (venture, corporate capex, loans) directed toward AI compute, data centers, tooling and related infrastructure.

nodes.label: Supply‑chain concentration
nodes.description: The degree to which critical inputs, suppliers and production stages for AI hardware and tools are concentrated among few nodes or regions.

nodes.label: Cross‑border technology transfer rate
nodes.description: The frequency and volume of technical knowledge, tooling, software and tacit engineering practices moving across national borders.

nodes.label: Export control intensity
nodes.description: The strictness and scope of trade restrictions, licensing regimes and export controls applied to AI‑relevant technologies and components.

nodes.label: Geopolitical security tension
nodes.description: The level of strategic rivalry, sanctions risk and political friction affecting cross‑border technology and investment relationships.

nodes.label: AI safety and incident frequency
nodes.description: The occurrence rate of safety, misuse, leak or major security incidents linked to AI models, deployments or development processes.

nodes.label: Energy supply reliability for data centers
nodes.description: The stability and availability of electrical power and grid capacity that can be committed to data centers and compute facilities.

nodes.label: Renewable power share of infrastructure
nodes.description: The proportion of energy consumed by AI infrastructure that is sourced from renewable or low‑carbon energy sources.

nodes.label: AI skilled talent availability
nodes.description: The size and accessibility of the qualified workforce (engineers, researchers, operators) able to design, build and run advanced AI systems.

nodes.label: Chip and model R&D intensity
nodes.description: The rate of resources (person‑years, budgets) devoted to research and development for semiconductor design, tooling and AI model advancement.

nodes.label: Regulatory compliance costs for AI infrastructure
nodes.description: The economic burden (time, money, operational constraints) borne to meet safety, privacy, export and environmental regulations for AI infrastructure.

nodes.label: Cybersecurity risk level
nodes.description: The assessed likelihood and expected severity of cyber intrusions, data exfiltration, or system compromise affecting AI infrastructure.

nodes.label: Market demand for AI services
nodes.description: The aggregate demand from enterprises, consumers and governments for AI capabilities, models, and AI‑powered products and services.

nodes.label: Environmental externalities from infrastructure
nodes.description: The local and systemic environmental impacts (land use change, heat, emissions, water use) generated by large‑scale AI infrastructure build‑out.

Missile production capacity
nodes.description: The aggregate industrial capacity to manufacture offensive cruise and deep‑strike missiles per unit time.

nodes.label: Missile arsenal size
nodes.description: The total deployed and reserve inventory of offensive missile systems and munitions.

nodes.label: Weapon mass‑producibility
nodes.description: The ease, cost curve, and standardization level enabling mass production of advanced offensive weapons.

nodes.label: Private defense investment rate
nodes.description: The rate at which private capital is allocated to defence‑oriented firms and technologies.

nodes.label: Public defence spending level
nodes.description: The aggregate government budgetary commitment to defence procurement, R&D, and force sustainment.

nodes.label: AI‑driven economic output
nodes.description: The economic output attributable to AI adoption, measured as value added or GDP contribution from AI‑intensive sectors.

nodes.label: AI industry growth rate
nodes.description: The tempo of expansion in AI‑related firms, revenues, and employment over time.

nodes.label: Electricity demand level
nodes.description: The total electrical energy demand across the system per unit time.

nodes.label: Energy generation capacity
nodes.description: The total installed capacity to generate electricity across all sources.

nodes.label: Nuclear generation capacity
nodes.description: The installed electrical generation capacity derived from nuclear power facilities.

nodes.label: Gas generation capacity
nodes.description: The installed electrical generation capacity derived from gas‑fired infrastructure.

nodes.label: Fusion technology maturity
nodes.description: The technological readiness and commercial maturity of fusion energy and related high‑energy technologies.

nodes.label: Cross‑border capital flow rate
nodes.description: The net rate of international private and institutional capital movements into technology and energy sectors.

nodes.label: Technology diffusion rate
nodes.description: The speed at which dual‑use and military‑relevant technologies spread between actors and sectors.

nodes.label: Strategic alignment degree
nodes.description: The extent and strength of cooperative security alignments and coordinated strategic postures among actors as perceived in the system.

nodes.label: Arms‑control and norms strength
nodes.description: The robustness and enforcement capacity of formal and informal norms, treaties, and regulatory frameworks governing weapons and related technologies.

Sovereign bond yield level
nodes.description: The prevailing yield (interest rate) on benchmark sovereign bonds across the developed-market yield curve.

nodes.label: Corporate bond spread level
nodes.description: The average credit spread between corporate bonds and comparable-maturity sovereign bonds, reflecting compensation for credit and liquidity risk.

nodes.label: Policy interest rate
nodes.description: The short-term policy interest rate set by central banks that anchors short-term funding costs.

nodes.label: Monetary policy communication tone
nodes.description: The hawkishness or dovishness expressed in central-bank communications and forward guidance about future policy paths.

nodes.label: Headline inflation rate
nodes.description: The observed inflation rate for broad price indices (including energy and food) in the real economy.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Market and investor expectations of future inflation over short- and medium-term horizons.

nodes.label: Energy price level
nodes.description: The prevailing price level of major energy commodities (eg oil and gas) that transmits into production and headline inflation.

nodes.label: Government net bond supply
nodes.description: The net flow of government debt issuance into the market after accounting for maturities and routine operations.

nodes.label: Government bond buyback intensity
nodes.description: The scale and frequency of active government debt repurchase operations that remove outstanding bonds from the market.

nodes.label: Bond market liquidity
nodes.description: The ease and depth with which bond positions can be transacted without large price impact, across maturities and issuers.

nodes.label: Portfolio rebalancing flow
nodes.description: Net investor reallocations across asset classes (eg bonds to equities or cash) driven by yield, risk and strategic shifts.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flow
nodes.description: Net international financial flows into or out of developed-market fixed-income and related asset markets.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: Aggregate propensity of investors to accept risk, influencing demand for higher-yielding and riskier assets versus safe havens.

nodes.label: Credit market stress level
nodes.description: The degree of strain in credit markets measured by indicators such as widening funding spreads, issuance freezes and default pressures.

nodes.label: Safe-haven asset demand
nodes.description: The flow of investor demand into traditionally safe assets (eg high-grade sovereigns, gold) in response to risk or inflation shocks.

nodes.label: Term premium level
nodes.description: The compensation investors require for bearing duration risk over and above expected short-term rates across the yield curve.
